title: Bulbs in a row and bulbs side by side: how the layout of a circuit changes what each part gets

summary.text: Add a second bulb to a working circuit, and the first bulb gets dimmer. Add it another way, and nothing changes at all. The bulbs and the cells are the same, so only the wiring can explain it. A circuit with one path is called a series circuit. A circuit with several paths is called a parallel circuit, and every home is wired that way. In this unit you test both with real bulbs, find out why a thin filament glows while a thick wire stays cool, and learn why the arrow in a circuit diagram points the wrong way. You also learn why a fuse is a thin wire that is meant to break.
summary.art: Two small circuits on a table side by side: on the left two dim bulbs in one loop, on the right two bright bulbs each with its own wires to the cell holder.

intro.hook: Try this with a grown-up. Light one torch bulb with two AA cells. Now put a second bulb into the same loop, one after the other. Both bulbs still glow, but each one is much dimmer than the single bulb was. The cells did not change. Where did the brightness go?
intro.text: The wires decide how the push of the cells is shared. In this unit you build circuits with bulbs in a row and bulbs side by side, and you score how bright each one is. You unscrew one bulb to see which circuit survives. You find out why a bulb's thin filament glows and why a fuse is meant to melt. You also test an LED, which works only one way round, and you meet the guess that made every circuit diagram point the wrong way.
intro.art: A hand unscrewing one of two bulbs: in the circuit on the left both bulbs go dark, and in the circuit on the right the other bulb keeps glowing.

outcomes: I can build a series circuit and a parallel circuit with two or three bulbs, and say how bright the bulbs are in each.
I can predict what the other bulbs do when one bulb is taken out, in a series circuit and in a parallel circuit.
I can explain, using the idea of sharing the cell's push, why bulbs in a row are dimmer and bulbs side by side are not.
I can explain why a thin filament glows while the thick wire stays cool, using the word resistance.
I can draw a circuit diagram with the symbols for a cell, a bulb, a switch and a wire, and build a circuit from someone else's diagram.
I can say why the arrow in a circuit diagram is a guess from 1747, that electrons really move the other way and only slowly, and show that an LED lights one way round only.
I can explain what a short circuit is and how a fuse protects a home.
I can match switches in a row to 'both needed' and switches side by side to 'either one is enough', and design a circuit for each.

terms.meaning: How much electric charge flows past a point in the circuit each second. A bigger current means a bigger flow.
terms.example: When you add a second bulb in a row, the current in the loop gets smaller, so both bulbs glow dimly.
terms.art: A wire with small dots flowing along it, a few dots for a small current and many dots for a large one.

terms.meaning: The size of the push that a cell gives to the charges in a circuit. It is measured in volts.
terms.example: One AA cell pushes with 1.5 volts. Two in a row push with 3 volts. A wall socket in India pushes with 230 volts.
terms.art: Three batteries of growing size, labelled 1.5 volts, 3 volts and 230 volts, each with an arrow of growing length.

terms.meaning: A circuit where the parts are joined one after the other, so there is only one path. The same current goes through every part.
terms.example: Old festival light strings are often wired in series. When one bulb breaks, the whole string goes dark.
terms.art: A cell and three bulbs joined in one single loop, with one arrow running through all of them.

terms.meaning: A circuit where the parts are joined side by side, so the electricity has more than one path. Each part gets the full push of the cell.
terms.example: A fan and a tube light in one room are wired in parallel. You can switch off the light and the fan keeps turning.
terms.art: A cell with two bulbs on two separate paths, with arrows splitting at one end and joining again at the other.

terms.meaning: One of the separate paths in a parallel circuit.
terms.example: In a circuit with two bulbs side by side, each bulb is on its own branch.
terms.art: A circuit with two branches coloured differently, one through each bulb.

terms.meaning: The very thin coiled wire inside a bulb. It gets so hot that it glows.
terms.example: In a torch bulb you can see the filament as a tiny bright coil between two supports.
terms.art: A torch bulb cut open in a drawing, showing the tiny coiled filament held between two thick support wires.

terms.meaning: How much a part holds back the flow of electricity. A thin wire, a long wire or a pencil lead holds back more than a short thick copper wire.
terms.example: A bulb's filament has a lot of resistance. That is why it heats up and glows, while the copper wires to it stay cool.
terms.art: A wide pipe next to a very narrow pipe with the same water flowing, the narrow pipe shown glowing hot.

terms.meaning: A drawing of a circuit that uses standard symbols and straight lines for wires, so that anyone in the world can read it.
terms.example: An electrician reads a circuit diagram to see which parts are in a row and which are side by side.
terms.art: A neat circuit diagram of a cell, a switch and two bulbs drawn with symbols and straight lines.

terms.meaning: A small standard drawing that stands for a part. A circle with a cross inside is a bulb. A long line next to a short fat line is a cell.
terms.example: In every circuit diagram, a gap with a lever is the symbol for a switch.
terms.art: A row of four symbols with their names under them: cell, bulb, switch and wire.

terms.meaning: A path with almost no resistance that lets a very large current flow, because the wire joins the two ends of a cell, or two mains wires, directly.
terms.example: A loose wire that touches both ends of a cell makes a short circuit. The wire and the cell get hot very fast.
terms.art: A cell with a thick wire straight across it, a red warning sign, and wavy heat lines rising from the wire.

terms.meaning: A thin piece of wire placed in a circuit on purpose. If too much current flows, the fuse heats up and melts first, and that breaks the circuit.
terms.example: In the fuse of a plug, a thin wire melts when a fault makes the current too big, and the appliance stops.
terms.art: A small glass fuse with a thin wire inside, intact on the left and melted in the middle on the right.

terms.meaning: A light-emitting diode. It is a small light that makes light without a glowing filament, and it works only when the current goes through it one way.
terms.example: The small red light on a phone charger or a TV is an LED.
terms.art: A red LED with one long leg and one short leg, and a small flat edge on the rim of its case.

terms.meaning: A tiny particle with a negative charge, found in every atom. The moving charges in a metal wire are electrons.
terms.example: In a copper wire, electrons drift slowly along the wire when a cell is joined, less than a millimetre in a second.
terms.art: A magnified drawing of a copper wire with small dots drifting slowly along it between larger fixed atoms.

terms.meaning: The direction that circuit diagrams use for current, from the plus end of the cell, round the circuit, to the minus end. It is a rule agreed long ago, and the electrons really move the opposite way.
terms.example: On a diagram the arrow leaves the plus end of the cell. The electrons in the wire move towards that plus end.
terms.art: A circuit diagram with a big arrow marked 'conventional current' one way and a small arrow marked 'electrons' the opposite way.

explanations.concept: Series circuit: one path, one push shared out
explanations.definition: In a series circuit the parts are joined one after the other. The same current goes through every part, and the cell's push is shared between them.
explanations.description: With one bulb on two cells, the whole push of 3 volts goes to that bulb. Add a second bulb in the same loop, and the two bulbs must share the 3 volts, about 1.5 volts each. Two bulbs also make the path harder to get through, so less current flows round the loop. Less current and less push on each bulb means both glow dimly. The current is the same size in every part of the loop, so the first bulb does not use up the electricity before the second. If any part is taken out, the loop is broken everywhere, and every part stops.
examples: Two bulbs in a row glow dimly, and both go out if one is unscrewed.
Three AA cells in a torch are in series, so their pushes add up to 4.5 volts.
A switch in a torch is in series with the bulb, so opening the switch breaks the loop.

perspectives.explanation: Series means one path. If one part fails open, everything in the path stops, so electricians use series only where that is wanted, such as a switch with the light it controls.

explanations.art: A single loop with a cell and two bulbs, with a thick arrow running all the way round through both bulbs.

explanations.concept: Parallel circuit: more paths, a full push for each
explanations.definition: In a parallel circuit the parts are joined side by side. Each part has its own path to the cell and gets the cell's full push.
explanations.description: Each bulb side by side has its own two wires to the cell, so each bulb gets the whole 3 volts and glows as brightly as a bulb alone. The current from the cell splits at one end and joins again at the other. The cell gives out the sum of the currents in all the branches. So two bulbs side by side draw twice the current from the cells, and three bulbs draw three times, and the cells run down faster. If one bulb is taken out, the other branches still make complete loops, so they keep glowing.
examples: Two bulbs side by side are both as bright as one bulb alone.
All the lights and fans in a home are in parallel, so each gets the full 230 volts and each can be switched off alone.
As an example, if a cell lasts about 6 hours with one bulb, it lasts roughly 3 hours with two bulbs side by side. Real times vary with the cell and the bulb.

perspectives.explanation: Parallel gives every part the full push, and a fault in one branch does not stop the others. The price is that the cell or supply must give out more current in total.

explanations.art: A cell with two bulbs on two separate branches, each branch glowing brightly, and arrows splitting and joining at the two ends.

explanations.concept: Why a thin filament glows and a thick wire stays cool
explanations.definition: Resistance is how much a part holds back the flow of electricity. Where resistance is high, the flowing charges give up more energy as heat.
explanations.description: The wires in your circuit are thick copper, which holds back the flow very little, so almost no energy is given up in them. The filament is very thin and made of tungsten. It holds the flow back a lot, so the charges give up much of their energy there as heat. The filament of a bulb on the mains gets hot, at about 2,500 degrees Celsius, which is hotter than lava. A hot enough thing glows, as a heated iron rod glows red. A torch bulb filament is not so hot but works the same way. The same current goes through the wire and the filament, but the filament is where the energy goes.
examples: The wires to a bulb stay cool while the filament glows.
A long thin pencil lead in a loop makes the bulb dimmer, because the lead holds the flow back.
A fuse is a thin wire on purpose: it holds back the flow so much that it melts first.

perspectives.explanation: The bulb is filled with a gas that does not burn, or has air taken out, so the very hot filament does not burn up. Most of the energy still leaves as heat, and only a small part as light.

explanations.art: A drawing of a thick copper wire joined to a thin glowing filament, with the same row of dots moving through both.

explanations.definition: A longer or thinner conductor has more resistance than a shorter or thicker one made of the same material.
explanations.description: Imagine water flowing through a pipe. A long, narrow pipe lets less water through each second than a short, wide one, if the push is the same. Wires work in a similar way. If you add a long pencil lead into a loop with a bulb, the bulb glows less. If you slide the clip along the lead, you can change how much lead is in the loop, and so how bright the bulb is. A fan regulator or a light dimmer in a home does the same job, in a cleverer way.
examples: Sliding a clip along a pencil lead changes the bulb's brightness.
A long thin extension wire holds back the flow more than a short thick one.
A fan regulator changes how much current reaches the fan.

perspectives.explanation: Water in a pipe is only a picture. It helps with the idea of flow, but a real wire works through the pushes between charged particles, and the picture breaks down in other cases.

explanations.art: A bulb in a loop with a long pencil lead, and a clip sliding along the lead with the bulb glowing dim when the clip is far and bright when it is near.

explanations.definition: A circuit diagram is a drawing that uses standard symbols for the parts and straight lines for the wires.
explanations.description: A circuit is hard to read from a photograph, because the wires bend and cross. So engineers all over the world draw circuits with the same symbols. A cell is a long thin line next to a short thick line. The long line is the plus end. A bulb is a circle with a cross in it. A switch is a gap with a lever. A wire is a straight line. With a diagram you can see at once whether bulbs are in a row or side by side, and you can build a circuit that someone far away has drawn.
examples: Two bulbs in a row are drawn one after another on a single loop.
Two bulbs side by side are drawn on two branches between the same two points.
A switch is drawn as a gap with a lever, open or closed.
explanations.art: A circuit diagram of a cell, a switch and a bulb, with each symbol labelled and a small photo of the real part beside it.

explanations.definition: In a circuit diagram the arrow for current goes from the plus end of the cell round to the minus end. This is called conventional current. In a metal wire the moving charges are electrons, and they move the opposite way.
explanations.description: In 1747 Benjamin Franklin had to guess which way electricity moved, and he guessed it moved from plus to minus. Everyone drew arrows that way. In 1897 J. J. Thomson found the electron, which has a negative charge. Later work showed that the moving charges in a metal wire are electrons. They move from the minus end of the cell to the plus end, the opposite way to the arrows. Engineers kept Franklin's arrow, because millions of diagrams and rules already used it. The answers come out right whichever way you picture the flow, as long as you stick to one.
examples: The arrow on a circuit diagram leaves the plus end of the cell.
The electrons in the wire move towards the plus end.
An LED works only when it is joined so that the current goes into its long leg.

perspectives.explanation: Learn the diagram rule first, because that is what you will see in books and exams. Then remember that the electrons really go the other way.

explanations.art: A circuit diagram with a large arrow going from the plus end of the cell, and a smaller row of dots going the opposite way.

explanations.concept: Electrons crawl, but the bulb lights at once
explanations.definition: The electrons in a wire drift very slowly, less than a millimetre each second. The push that sets them moving travels along the wire at a large fraction of the speed of light.
explanations.description: When you close a switch, the bulb lights at once. This is not because an electron raced from the cell to the bulb. The wire is already full of electrons. When the cell pushes the electrons at its end, the push passes along the wire from one to the next almost instantly, like a row of marbles in a tube. Every electron in the loop starts to drift together, including the ones in the filament. Their drifting is slow, but the bulb does not need to wait for a particular electron to arrive.
examples: A long extension wire does not delay a bulb at its end.
A row of marbles in a tube moves at once at both ends when you push one end.
A call from Chennai to Delhi along a wire arrives in a fraction of a second.

perspectives.explanation: A better picture is that the cell sets up an electric field along the whole wire, and the field pushes all the electrons at once.

explanations.art: A long glass tube full of marbles with a hand pushing in the first marble at one end and the last marble moving out at the other end.

explanations.definition: A short circuit is a path with almost no resistance that lets a very large current flow. A fuse is a thin wire in a circuit that melts if the current gets too big, and so breaks the circuit.
explanations.description: If a bare wire joins the two ends of a cell, there is nothing to hold the flow back except the wire. The current is huge, and the wire, and the cell, heat up fast. At home the same can happen if two mains wires touch, and the heat can start a fire. So a fuse or a trip switch, called a miniature circuit breaker or MCB, is put in the circuit. It has a thin part that heats first. When the current is too big, the fuse melts or the MCB flips, and the loop is broken before the wires get dangerous. A fuse protects the wires. It does not protect a person who is touching a live wire.
examples: A fuse in the plug of an appliance melts when a fault makes the current too large.
An MCB in the box near the main door trips and clicks off.
A bulb with a wire across its two ends goes dark, because the current takes the easy path.

perspectives.explanation: A fuse or an MCB is chosen to match the wire. A thin wire must have a small fuse. Putting in a bigger fuse, or a bit of wire in its place, is dangerous because the house wiring will then overheat first.

explanations.art: A house wiring box with an MCB switch flipped down, and beside it a melted fuse wire inside a small glass tube.

explanations.concept: Why homes are wired in parallel, and switches in series
explanations.definition: In a home, every light and appliance is on its own branch, in parallel, so each gets the full 230 volts. Each switch is in series with the light it controls.
explanations.description: If a home were wired in series, switching off one light would turn off every light. And each lamp would get only a small share of the 230 volts. So a home has a pair of wires from the supply, and each light, fan or socket is joined across that pair. Each is in its own branch. The switch for a light sits in the same branch as the light, one after the other. Opening the switch breaks only that branch.
examples: Switching off the kitchen light leaves the fan on.
Two switches in a row, both closed, are needed to light a bulb.
Two switches side by side, either closed, will light a bulb.
explanations.art: A simple plan of a room with two supply wires running along the wall, and a light with its switch, a fan and a socket, each on its own branch.

explanations.concept: Where does the energy of a circuit travel?
explanations.description: The usual picture is that the electrons carry energy along the wire to the bulb. A second picture comes from John Henry Poynting, who worked it out in 1884. He showed that the energy of a circuit flows through the space around the wire, in the electric and magnetic fields, and then sinks into the wire and the bulb. Both pictures give the same results for any circuit you can build. Some physics teachers think the second picture is closer to what really happens. Others say it is not needed at this level. It is an idea to keep open, and not a thing to memorise.
examples: Energy reaches a bulb just as quickly through a long wire as through a short one.
A power line carries energy over many kilometres with its electrons drifting very slowly.
A wireless charger moves energy through the space between two coils.

perspectives.explanation: The energy travels inside the wire, carried along by the moving electrons.
The energy travels in the fields around the wire, and the wire guides it to the bulb.

explanations.art: A wire with two pictures beside it: one with glowing dots moving along inside the wire, and one with soft arrows flowing in from the space around the wire.

agreed.text: In a series circuit the same current goes through every part, and in a parallel circuit each branch gets the full voltage of the cell.
agreed.evidence: Meters placed in different parts of circuits show the same current all round a series loop, and the same voltage across each branch of a parallel circuit.

agreed.text: A bulb's filament glows because it holds back the current so much that it gets very hot.
agreed.evidence: The colour of the light tells us the temperature. A filament in a mains bulb glows at about 2,500 degrees Celsius, and tungsten does not melt until 3,422 degrees.

agreed.text: The moving charges in a metal wire are electrons, and they move from the minus end of the cell to the plus end.
agreed.evidence: Thomson found the electron in 1897. Later experiments on metals showed that the charges carried in a wire are negative.

agreed.text: A short circuit lets a very large current flow, and a fuse or MCB protects the wiring by breaking the circuit.
agreed.evidence: Electrical safety standards require fuses and breakers matched to the wire, because overheated wires cause fires, and tests show they cut the current in time.

agreed.text: Two switches in a row need both to be closed, and two switches side by side need only one.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can test this with a cell, a bulb and two paper-clip switches. Claude Shannon showed in 1937 that this is how computer logic is built from switches.

challenging.claim: The bulb uses up the electricity, so less comes out of the bulb than goes in.
challenging.who: Many learners, and some old books.
challenging.for: A cell does run out, and a bulb seems to 'use' electricity.
challenging.against: Meters show the same current going into a bulb and coming out. What runs out of the cell is its stored energy, and the bulb turns that energy into heat and light.

challenging.claim: In a row of bulbs, the first bulb is the brightest, because the electricity reaches it first.
challenging.for: It seems natural that the first bulb should get the most.
challenging.against: The same current goes through every bulb in a row, so equal bulbs glow equally. Only the order along the wire is different.

challenging.claim: The arrows in a circuit diagram show which way the electrons move.
challenging.for: The arrow goes round the circuit like a flow, and it is natural to think it shows what is moving.
challenging.against: The arrow follows a rule that Benjamin Franklin guessed in 1747. In a metal wire the electrons move the opposite way.

challenging.claim: Thomas Edison invented the electric light bulb.
challenging.for: In 1879 and 1880 his team in the USA made a long-lasting lamp and built the wiring, meters and generators to sell light to whole streets.
challenging.against: Joseph Swan in England showed a working lamp with a carbon filament in 1878 and 1879. Lewis Latimer, a Black draughtsman and engineer, patented a better way to make carbon filaments in 1882. Many people improved the bulb over many years.

big_questions.q: The same bulb was bright alone, dim in a row and dark when there was a gap. Which of these is the real bulb?
big_questions.hint: Think about what changed, and what stayed the same. Is brightness a fact about the bulb, or about the whole loop?

big_questions.q: In a row, the first bulb does not use up the electricity before it reaches the second. So what does each bulb take from the cell?
big_questions.hint: The current is the same all round the loop. Think about what the cell gave to the charges at the start, and what they have less of after each bulb.

big_questions.q: The electrons in a wire move less than a millimetre in a second, yet a bulb lights the moment you close the switch. What is it that travels fast?
big_questions.hint: Think about a long tube full of marbles. Push one in at one end.

big_questions.q: The same current goes through the thick wire and the thin filament. Why does only the filament glow?
big_questions.hint: Where does the push of the cell get used up? Think of a crowd squeezing through a narrow gate.

big_questions.q: India's power grid was joined into one national grid in 2013, and in 2012 a failure left about 600 million people without power. Is one big joined grid safer or riskier than many small ones?
big_questions.hint: A joined grid can share power when one place fails. But a failure can also spread. List one good and one bad side.

big_questions.q: Which things you depend on are like bulbs in a row, where one break stops everything, and which are like bulbs side by side?
big_questions.hint: Think of a train with its carriages, a school day, a kitchen, and a village's water supply.

big_questions.q: Franklin's guess about the direction of electricity turned out to be backwards, but engineers kept using it. When is it sensible to keep an old rule you know is a convention?
big_questions.hint: Think about all the diagrams, books and machines that already use it. Think about which way the Sun 'rises' in the sentence we all use.

big_questions.q: An electric eel stacks thousands of tiny cells in a row, and their small pushes add up to a very large one. What else in nature adds small pushes together?
big_questions.hint: Think of a crowd clapping, an ant colony, ripples on a pond, or a million raindrops filling a river.

story.title: Forty-Six Bulbs
text: On the evening of Karthigai Deepam, the lane in Madurai where Meenakshi lived looked like a different place. Every house had a row of clay lamps on the steps. The women had drawn kolams at every door. And across the lane, from the neem tree to the tea stall, Murugan mama had hung a long string of small coloured bulbs. There were forty-six of them. Meenakshi was nine, and she had counted them twice with him that afternoon.

At six o'clock the whole street gathered on the steps. Murugan mama pushed the plug into the socket by the pole, and the string came alive. It glowed red, yellow, green and blue. Everyone clapped. Meenakshi's grandmother, Paati, lit the biggest lamp on their step, and the flame leaned and settled.
Ten minutes later, there was a tiny pop, and the whole string went dark. Not one bulb. All forty-six, at the same moment. The clay lamps went on flickering, but the lane suddenly felt empty.

"Power cut!" someone shouted. But Paati pointed to the tube light over the tea stall, which was still shining, and to the TV in the house next door, which was still talking. "Not a power cut," she said. "Only our string."

Murugan mama checked the plug. He checked the box on the pole. He walked along the string, tugging each wire. "Maybe a rat chewed it," said one neighbour. "Maybe it is bad luck," said another. The big lamp ceremony was at seven o'clock, and Murugan mama was starting to sweat.

Meenakshi stood very still. She was remembering the science corner at school. Last week, Lakshmi miss had given her group a cell, two bulbs and some wires. They had put both bulbs into one loop. When Farhan had unscrewed one bulb, the other one had gone dark too. Farhan had said it was magic. Lakshmi miss had said, "No. There is one path, and you broke it."
"Mama," said Meenakshi, "is every bulb on this string joined one after the other, in one long path?"
"Of course," said Murugan mama. "One wire runs through all of them. That is how strings are made."

"Then it is like our school circuit. If one bulb is broken inside, the path is broken for every bulb. They all go out together." She looked at the string. "Mama, the string is not dead. Only one bulb is."
Murugan mama opened his mouth, and shut it again. Then he laughed. "But which one? There are forty-six!"

"First pull out the plug," said Paati, in the voice she used for important things. "Nobody touches a bulb on a string that is plugged in. This is the wall current. It is not a small cell." Murugan mama pulled the plug out by its plastic body, and set it on the step.

Meenakshi took her mother's phone and switched on the torch. "A good bulb has a tiny coil of thread inside, joined at both ends," she said. "A broken one has a gap in the thread." She and her friend Farhan took half of the string each. They held each bulb up to the torch light and looked in, one after another, down the lane. Murugan mama held the wire steady.
At the thirty-first bulb, Farhan stopped. "Here! The thread is broken. There is a gap in the middle."
Murugan mama had a spare bulb in his shirt pocket from last year. He twisted out the dead bulb and put in the new one. Paati checked that his hands were dry. Then he pushed in the plug.
All forty-six bulbs came on at once. The lane cheered so loudly that the crows flew out of the neem tree.

"Each bulb takes only a small share of the push, you know," said Murugan mama, when the noise had settled. "The wall pushes with two hundred and thirty volts, and that is divided between forty-six bulbs. That is why such tiny bulbs can live on it."
"Next year," said Meenakshi, "we could give every bulb its own pair of wires to the main wire. Then if one broke, only that one would go dark."
"More wire, more work," said Murugan mama.
"But the big lamp would start on time," said Paati. And she handed Meenakshi the first match.
story.epiphany: In a string wired in one path, one broken bulb breaks the path for every bulb. If each bulb has its own path, a broken bulb puts out only itself.
ask: Why does a whole string of bulbs wired in one path go dark when only one bulb is broken?
How could you wire the same bulbs so that a broken bulb puts out only itself?
Why must a mains string be unplugged before anyone touches the bulbs?
art: A lane in Madurai at dusk with clay lamps on the steps, kolams at the doors, and a long string of coloured bulbs hung from a neem tree to a tea stall.
The same lane with the string suddenly dark, a few clay lamps flickering, and a worried man looking along the wire.
A girl and a boy holding bulbs up to a phone torch on the lane, looking inside each one, with the plug lying on a step.
The lane with all forty-six bulbs glowing, a grandmother handing a girl a match, and crows flying out of the neem tree.
story.note: A made-up story. The science in it is real. Old festival strings wired in one path do go dark when one bulb breaks. Many newer strings have a tiny extra wire in each bulb that closes the gap, so a string may not fail this way. Forty-six bulbs of about 5 volts each would use up the 230 volts of the mains. Only grown-ups ever touch a mains string, and the plug is pulled out first.
