items.f: One cell and two equal bulbs in a row. How bright is each bulb, compared with one bulb alone?
items.b: Dimmer. The two bulbs share the cell's push, so each gets about half.

items.f: One cell and two equal bulbs side by side. How bright is each bulb, compared with one bulb alone?
items.b: The same as one bulb alone. Each bulb has its own path and gets the whole push.

items.f: Two bulbs are in a row. You unscrew one. What does the other bulb do?
items.b: It goes out. The only path is broken.

items.f: Two bulbs are side by side. You unscrew one. What does the other bulb do?
items.b: It stays lit. Its own path is still whole.

items.f: A cell, a bulb and a switch are in one loop. The switch is open. Is the bulb lit?
items.b: No. An open switch is a gap in the only path.

items.f: A cell and a bulb are in a loop. A thick wire is joined straight across the two sides of the bulb. Does the bulb light?
items.b: No. The current takes the easy path through the thick wire, and the bulb gets almost nothing. The wire and cell may get hot.

items.f: Three bulbs are in a row. The middle bulb has a broken thread. Do the other two light?
items.b: No. The break in the middle breaks the one path for all three.

items.f: Two cells are in a row, facing the same way, with one bulb. Is the bulb brighter or dimmer than with one cell?
items.b: Brighter. The pushes add up, 1.5 volts plus 1.5 volts makes 3 volts.

items.f: Two cells are in a row but facing opposite ways, with one bulb. What does the bulb do?
items.b: It stays dark. The pushes work against each other and cancel.

items.f: Two cells are joined side by side, with one bulb. Compared with one cell, how bright is the bulb and how long does the pair last?
items.b: The same brightness. The two cells last about twice as long, because they share the work.

items.f: A string of forty-six festival bulbs goes dark when one bulb breaks. How are the bulbs joined?
items.b: In a row, in one path. One break stops all of them.

items.f: A home has a fan and a tube light. The tube light is switched off. What does the fan do?
items.b: It keeps turning. They are in parallel, each on its own branch.

items.f: An LED is joined with its legs the wrong way round. Does it light? Is it broken?
items.b: It does not light, but it is not broken. Turn it round and it lights.

items.f: A bulb and two switches are all in one row. When does the bulb light?
items.b: Only when both switches are closed. Both are needed.

items.f: A bulb is joined with two switches side by side. When does the bulb light?
items.b: When either switch is closed, or both. One is enough.

items.f: The same current goes through a thick wire and a thin filament. Which one gets hotter?
items.b: The thin filament. It holds the flow back more, so more energy turns to heat there.

items.f: A wire joins the two ends of a cell directly, with nothing else in the loop. What happens?
items.b: A very large current flows. The wire and cell get hot fast. This is a short circuit, and it is dangerous.

items.f: A fuse in a house wire melts. Is that a good thing or a bad thing?
items.b: A good thing. It broke the circuit before the wires overheated.

items.f: Three bulbs are side by side. You take two of them out. What does the third do?
items.b: It glows just as bright as before. Its path is not changed.

items.f: A long pencil lead is added to a loop with a bulb. What happens to the bulb?
items.b: It gets dimmer. The lead holds back the flow.

items.f: On a circuit diagram, the arrow goes from the plus end of the cell round to the minus end. Which way do the electrons in the wire really go?
items.b: From minus to plus, the opposite way. The arrow is a rule Franklin guessed in 1747.

items.f: A torch has three AA cells in a row, all facing the same way. How many volts do they push with?
items.b: 4.5 volts. Each cell adds 1.5 volts.

items.f: An electric eel's body has thousands of tiny cells stacked in a row. Why does a row make a large push?
items.b: In a row, the small pushes add up, as the cells in a torch do.

items.f: When you close a switch, the bulb lights at once. Does an electron race from the cell to the bulb?
items.b: No. The wire is already full of electrons. They all start to drift together, very slowly.

rules: One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader does not show the back.
Every other player says an answer and a reason, out loud. They may draw the circuit on paper first.
The reader reads the back. A right answer scores one point. A good reason scores one more point.
The reader's job passes to the next player after each card.
Playing alone: say your answer and reason out loud, then check the back. Score your own points out of 48.
The game ends when all the cards have been read. The player with the most points wins. Playing alone, try to beat your last score.

flow.do: Cut out the 24 cards and shuffle them into a pile. Make a score sheet with each player's name. Show your child the front and the back of one card.
flow.say: Each card asks a question about a circuit. The back has the answer and the reason. The reader reads the front. Everyone else says an answer and a reason.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Shuffle them. Each card has a circuit question on the front.
flow.parent: Cards are printed two-sided. If you cannot print two-sided, stick each answer on the back by hand.
flow.context: In this step, you set up the Circuit Detectives game.

flow.do: Play the first 8 cards. After each card the reader reads the back aloud. Score one point for the right answer and one more for a good reason. After card three, ask the question below.
flow.say: The reader reads the front. Everyone says an answer and a reason. Then the reader reads the back. One point for the answer. One more for the reason.
flow.kid: The reader reads a card. Say an answer and a reason. Check the back.

ask.q: What do the cards where a bulb stays lit have in common?
good: Each bulb has its own path.
The break is in a different branch.

flow.parent: Let children argue their reasons before the back is read. A right answer with a weak reason earns one point. A good reason is worth the second.
flow.context: In this step, you play the first eight cards and learn how to score.

flow.do: Play the next 16 cards. Keep the scores. If a card is hard, draw the circuit on paper to work it out.
flow.say: Keep going. If a card is hard, draw the circuit with the symbols. Is the bulb in a row, or side by side? Can the current find a whole loop?
flow.kid: Keep playing. Draw the circuit if a card is hard.
flow.context: In this step, you play the rest of the cards and draw circuits to help.

flow.do: Add up the scores. Ask which card was the hardest, and why. Put the cards the child got wrong back in the pile and try them again.
flow.say: Add up the points. Which card was hardest? What would you draw to work it out? Let us try the hard ones again.
flow.kid: Add up your points. Try the hard cards again.
flow.context: This is the last step of Circuit Detectives. You count points and replay the hard cards.

experiments.title: Bulb Teams: bulbs in a row or side by side?
experiments.question: What happens to the brightness of the bulbs when you add a second and a third bulb, in a row and side by side? What happens to the others when you take one out?
experiments.predict: Before you build anything, guess. How bright will two bulbs in a row be, compared with one bulb alone? How bright will two bulbs side by side be? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same two fresh cells and the same kind of bulb every time. Test in the same dim room, after your eyes have rested for one minute. Only the layout changes. The single bulb is the control and always scores 5. Ask a second person to score the bulbs too, without seeing your scores. If you both give the same score, you can trust it.
results_table: Do the bulbs look the same?
Unscrew one bulb: what do the others do?

materials.item: 2 fresh AA cells in a holder, or two cells joined with tape and wire
3 torch bulbs, 2.5 volts, each in a bulb holder
about 8 insulated wires with bare ends or crocodile clips, some short and some long
2 or 3 spare torch bulbs from the same packet, in case one is faulty or does not match
a room that can be made dim
the results table and a pencil

experiments.safety: Use only AA cells, never a wall socket or a plug. Disconnect the cells after each test. Bulbs can be warm after a minute, so touch only the holders. Do not use cells that look swollen or leaking.
experiments.record: For each layout, write the score of each bulb from 0 to 5, and what the others did when you unscrewed one. Then draw a bar chart with one bar for each layout.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you light bulbs in different layouts on the same two cells, and find out how bright each one is.

setup.art: A cell holder with two AA cells, one torch bulb in a holder and two wires making a loop, the bulb glowing brightly on a table in a dim room.
setup.caption: 1. One bulb on two cells. This is the control and scores 5.

setup.art: Two bulbs in holders joined one after the other in a single loop with the cell holder, both glowing dimly.
setup.caption: 2. Two bulbs in a row: one path, through the first bulb and then the second.

setup.art: Three bulbs in holders in a single loop with the cell holder, glowing very faintly red.
setup.caption: 3. Three bulbs in a row.

setup.art: Two bulbs side by side: short wires joining their left sides and their right sides, and the cell holder joined to both, both bulbs glowing brightly.
setup.caption: 4. Two bulbs side by side: each bulb has its own path to the cells.

setup.art: A hand unscrewing one of two bulbs in a side-by-side circuit while the other stays lit, next to the same in a row circuit with both dark.
setup.caption: 5. Unscrew one bulb and watch the others.

flow.do: Show your child the cells, the three bulbs and the wires. Ask for a guess about each layout before you build anything. Write each guess as a score from 0 to 5 in the table.
flow.say: We will light one bulb, then two in a row, then three in a row. Then we will put bulbs side by side. How bright will each be, compared with one bulb alone? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess first. Will two bulbs be dimmer? Will three? Say why.

ask.q: Why do you think two bulbs in a row will be that bright?
good: Two bulbs need more electricity, so each gets less.
They will be brighter, because there are more bulbs.

flow.parent: Do not correct any guess. Many children say two bulbs will be brighter, because there are more of them. Score the single bulb as 5. Write each guess as a score from 0 to 5. With 2 to 4 children, one builds, one scores, one keeps the table and one draws; swap jobs for each layout. Each child writes their own guess before anyone speaks.
flow.context: This is the first step of Bulb Teams. You guess before you build.

flow.do: Dim the room. Build one loop with the cell holder, a bulb and two wires. Wait one minute for your eyes to adjust. This glow is the control and scores 5.
flow.say: Switch off the room light and draw the curtains. Join the cells to one bulb. This is our control. Look at how bright it is. It scores five.
flow.kid: Dim the room. Light one bulb. This bulb scores 5.
flow.parent: Use fresh cells and 2.5 volt bulbs. If the room cannot be made dark, cup a hand round each bulb and score every layout in the same way. Never leave a circuit joined for more than a minute. The cells run down. Cheap bulbs are often not quite equal, so light each bulb alone first and use the three that look most alike. Damp weather can make clips and bulb holders touch badly, so press each joint firmly.
flow.context: In this step, you light one bulb to see what a normal glow looks like.

flow.do: Join a second bulb into the same loop, so the electricity goes through one bulb and then the other. Score each bulb from 0 to 5. Write whether the two look the same.
flow.say: Put the second bulb in the same loop, one after the other. Is it brighter or dimmer than the single bulb? Is the first bulb brighter than the second? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Add a second bulb in the same loop. Score both bulbs. Is the first one brighter?

ask.q: What do you notice about the first bulb and the second bulb?
good: Both are dimmer than one bulb alone.
Neither is brighter than the other.

flow.parent: Typically both bulbs glow equally, with a dull orange light, clearly dimmer than the single bulb. Exact brightness depends on your cells and bulbs. If neither glows, check that the bulbs are 2.5 volts and the cells are fresh, and that every wire is touching bare metal.

check.q: Both bulbs in a row glow equally dimly. What does that show about the electricity going through the first bulb?
options: The second bulb is broken
The first bulb used up the electricity, and the second used the rest
The same flow goes through both bulbs, so the first one did not use it up
check.why: If the first bulb used up the electricity, the second would be darker. Equal glow shows the same flow reaches both. If your bulbs did look different, one may be a different kind of bulb, so check them one at a time.

flow.context: In this step, you put two bulbs in a row and compare them with the single bulb.

flow.do: Join a third bulb into the same loop. Score all three bulbs. They may glow only faintly, or not at all. Write down what you see.
flow.say: Add a third bulb in the same loop. What do you see? If you see no glow, look closely, and shade the bulb with your hand. No glow is a good result too.
flow.kid: Add a third bulb in the row. Score it. No glow is a result too.

ask.q: What pattern do you see as you add bulbs in a row?
good: They all share the same cells.

flow.parent: With three 2.5 volt bulbs on 3 volts, each bulb gets about 1 volt. The glow may be a faint red thread, or nothing. Do not worry. Write down what you saw. Disconnect the cells.
flow.context: In this step, you add a third bulb in the row and look for a pattern.

flow.do: Take the loop apart. Join the left sides of two bulb holders with one short wire. Join the right sides with another. Join the cell holder to the left and right sides. Score both bulbs. Add a third bulb the same way.
flow.say: Now give each bulb its own path. Join the two left sides with a wire, and the two right sides with a wire. Then join the cells to the left and the right. How bright are the bulbs now?
flow.kid: Join the bulbs side by side. Each gets its own path. Score them.

ask.q: How is this circuit different from the row?
good: Each bulb has its own way to the cell.

flow.parent: Expect both bulbs to be about as bright as the single bulb, and a third bulb the same. Disconnect the cells after each test. Side by side, the cells run down faster, and the wires may feel a little warm. Use only the holder to touch hot bulbs.
flow.context: In this step, you wire the bulbs side by side, so that each bulb has its own path to the cells.

flow.do: Join two bulbs in a row again. Unscrew one bulb a little and watch the other. Then do the same with two bulbs side by side. Write down what the other bulb did each time.
flow.say: Predict first. If I unscrew one bulb in the row, what will the other bulb do? And side by side? Now try each, and watch.
flow.kid: Unscrew one bulb. What does the other bulb do? Try the row, then side by side.
flow.parent: In the row, both bulbs go out. Side by side, the other bulb stays as bright as before. Bulbs are usually only warm at 3 volts, but hold them by their holders. If the bulb in the row circuit stays lit when you unscrew the other, a wire is bridging the holder: check the wiring.

check.q: A string of festival lights goes completely dark when one bulb fails. How are its bulbs most likely joined?
options: They are not joined to a cell
In a row, in one single path
Side by side, each with its own path
check.why: In a row, one broken bulb breaks the only path, so every bulb goes out. If the bulbs were side by side, only the broken one would go dark. A string that goes dark as a whole is wired in a row.

flow.context: In this step, you take one bulb out of each layout and see what happens to the others.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they thought (claim), what they saw (evidence), and why (reasoning). Write one line for each. Then ask them to draw both circuits.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you saw, and why. Then draw both circuits.
flow.parent: A strong answer says the same flow goes through every bulb in the row and the cells' push is shared between them, so each bulb gets less. Side by side, each bulb has its own path and gets the whole push. After they have said what they saw, explain it. Two bulbs make the path harder, so less flow goes round, and each bulb gets about half of the 3 volts. Side by side, each bulb gets all 3 volts, but the cells give out twice as much flow, so they run down about twice as fast.
flow.think: If the first bulb in a row does not use up the electricity, what makes the bulbs dim?
flow.context: This is the last step of Bulb Teams. You explain your results.

experiments.title: Which Way Round? A bulb and an LED
experiments.question: Does a bulb light when you turn the cell round? Does an LED?
experiments.predict: Before you test, guess. Will the bulb light with the cell turned round? Will the LED? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same cell and the same wires for every test. Only the direction changes. Try each way twice, because a loose wire can fool you. If the LED does not light either way, check the legs touch the faces of the cell and do not touch each other.

materials.item: 2 AA cells in a holder, with a 2.5 volt bulb in a holder and 2 wires
1 coin cell of 3 volts, such as a CR2032
2 red LEDs, 5 millimetres wide, with legs of different lengths
sticky tape
the results table and a pencil

experiments.safety: A coin cell can badly hurt a child who swallows it, so a grown-up holds it and keeps it from children under five. Put it back in its packet and tape the packet when done. Never join an LED straight to two AA cells, because the current is too big and the LED burns out.
experiments.record: In the table, write what the bulb did and what the LED did with the cell each way round. Draw an LED and mark which leg is plus.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you test whether a bulb and an LED care about which way round the cell is joined.

setup.art: A bulb circuit with the cells joined one way and, beside it, the same circuit with the cell holder turned round, both bulbs glowing equally.
setup.caption: 1. Light the bulb. Turn the cells round. Compare.

setup.art: A close-up of a red LED showing the long leg marked plus and the short leg marked minus.
setup.caption: 2. Find the long leg and the short leg of the LED.

setup.art: An adult's fingers holding a coin cell, with an LED's long leg touching the plus face and the short leg touching the other face, and the LED glowing.
setup.caption: 3. A grown-up holds the cell. Long leg to plus, short leg to minus.

setup.art: The same LED turned round on the coin cell and dark, next to two LEDs taped to a coin cell facing opposite ways with only one glowing.
setup.caption: 4. Turn the LED round. Then try two LEDs facing opposite ways.

flow.do: Show your child the bulb circuit, the LED and the coin cell. Keep the coin cell in your hand. Ask for a guess about each part, and the reason.
flow.say: A bulb and an LED are both lights. If I turn the cell round, will the bulb still light? Will the LED? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess first. Does the cell's direction matter for a bulb? For an LED? Why?
flow.parent: Do not correct any guess. Write the guesses in the table. A coin cell can be swallowed. Keep it in your hand or on a tray, and away from children under five.
flow.context: This is the first step of Which Way Round. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Join a bulb to the cell holder, and watch it light. Score its brightness from 0 to 5. Turn the cell holder round, or swap the two wires on the cells. Score it again. Write down what you see both ways.
flow.say: Light the bulb. Now swap the two wires on the cells, so the cells face the other way. Does the bulb change? Is it as bright as before?
flow.kid: Light the bulb. Swap the wires on the cells. What changes?

ask.q: Does the bulb care which end of the cell the wire touches?
good: It looks the same both ways.

flow.parent: The bulb should glow just the same both ways. The filament does not mind which way the current goes.
flow.context: In this step, you test a bulb with the cell facing one way and then the other.

flow.do: A grown-up holds the coin cell. Look at the LED. Find the long leg and the short leg. Touch the long leg to the cell's flat side marked plus. Touch the short leg to the other face of the cell. Write down what you see.
flow.say: Hold the LED by its legs. One leg is longer. Touch the long leg to the plus face of the cell. Touch the short leg to the other face. What happens?
flow.kid: A grown-up holds the cell. Long leg to plus. Short leg to minus. Look!
flow.parent: The long leg is the plus leg. The coin cell has a plus face with writing on it and a flat minus face. If nothing happens, check the legs are touching the faces and not each other. A fresh coin cell typically gives a clear red glow. Keep the bent legs off the metal rim of the cell, because the rim joins to the plus face and the LED would be shorted and stay dark. If it is still dark, try the other LED or a new coin cell. With 2 to 4 children, only the grown-up holds the cell: the children take turns as the one who turns the LED, the one who records, and the one who draws. Put the cell back in its packet when you are finished.
flow.context: In this step, you light an LED from a coin cell, one way round.

flow.do: Turn the LED round, so the long leg touches the minus face and the short leg touches the plus face. Watch it. Turn it back. Do this twice. Write down what you see each time.
flow.say: Now turn the LED round the other way. Does it light? Turn it back. Is anything damaged? What does this tell you about how the electricity moves through an LED?
flow.kid: Turn the LED round. Does it light? Turn it back.
flow.parent: The LED will not light the wrong way round, and it is not damaged. The wrong way round stops the current.

check.q: Your LED lit with the long leg on the plus face and stayed dark when turned round. What does this show?
options: The cell ran out after the first try
An LED lets current through in one direction only
The LED broke when it was turned round
check.why: If the cell had run out, the LED would also stay dark when turned back. It lit again, so the cell was fine. An LED is a one-way part. A wrong-way LED is not broken. It only blocks the current.

flow.context: In this step, you try the LED the wrong way round, then the right way again.

flow.do: A grown-up tapes two LEDs to the coin cell facing opposite ways. One has its long leg on the plus face. The other has its long leg on the minus face. Look at which one lights. Then turn the coin cell over.
flow.say: Two LEDs, facing opposite ways, on one cell. Which one will light? Now I turn the cell over. What will happen? Why?
flow.kid: Two LEDs face opposite ways. Which lights? Turn the cell over. Now which?
flow.parent: Only one LED lights. When the cell is turned over, the other LED lights and the first goes dark. If both stay dark, check that each LED has one leg on each face.
flow.context: In this step, you use two LEDs facing opposite ways to see the one-way rule twice.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw, and why. Tell them that the arrow in circuit diagrams is a guess from 1747. Ask which way they think the electrons go.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think? What did you see? Why do you think it happened? Which part does not care which way round the cell is, and which part does?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you saw, and why. Draw an LED with its long leg marked plus.
flow.parent: A strong answer says the bulb's thin wire heats whichever way the current goes, but an LED has a special material inside that lets current through one way only. After they have answered, tell them that the arrow in a diagram, from plus to minus, was guessed by Benjamin Franklin in 1747. The electrons in a wire go the other way.
flow.think: If a bulb works both ways, but an LED works one way, what must be different inside an LED?
flow.context: This is the last step of Which Way Round. You explain your results.

activities.title: Draw It Like an Engineer: circuit diagrams

materials.item: paper, a pencil and a ruler
the circuit parts from Bulb Teams

activities.record: Keep your diagrams. Stick them in your notebook next to a photo of each circuit.
activities.context: In this activity, you learn the four symbols used in circuit diagrams and draw the circuits that you built.

setup.art: Four circuit symbols drawn large on a sheet of paper, each with its name written underneath: cell, bulb, switch, wire.
setup.caption: 1. Learn the four symbols.

setup.art: A neat ruled diagram of two bulbs side by side with a cell, next to the real circuit on the table.
setup.caption: 2. Draw each circuit you built.

setup.art: Two children swapping their drawings and building each other's circuit on a table.
setup.caption: 3. Swap drawings and build your partner's circuit.

flow.do: Show the four symbols on a piece of paper: cell, bulb, switch and wire. Say what each one means. Ask your child to copy each symbol twice.
flow.say: Engineers draw circuits with the same four symbols all over the world. A cell is a long line and a short fat line. The long line is the plus end. A bulb is a circle with a cross. A switch is a gap with a lever. A wire is a straight line.
flow.kid: Learn four symbols. Cell, bulb, switch, wire. Copy each one twice.

ask.q: Which end of the cell is the long line?

flow.parent: Write the symbols large on paper. Let your child copy them. The cell symbol can be tricky: long thin line for plus, short thick line for minus.
flow.context: In this step, you learn the four symbols that engineers use.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw three circuits from Bulb Teams as diagrams. Draw one bulb, two bulbs in a row, and two bulbs side by side. Use a ruler for the straight lines. Mark the plus end of the cell.
flow.say: Now draw each circuit you built, using the symbols. Use a ruler for the wires. In the row, the bulbs are on one loop. Side by side, each bulb has its own branch.
flow.kid: Draw your three circuits with the symbols. Use a ruler for wires.
flow.parent: If they did not do Bulb Teams, build the circuits quickly, or look at the picture steps of it. Check that the row has one loop and the side-by-side drawing has two branches joining the same two points.

check.q: In a diagram, two bulbs are drawn on two separate branches between the same two points. Which circuit is this?
options: Parallel
A short circuit
Series
check.why: Two branches between the same points means the electricity has two paths. That is parallel. A series circuit has only one loop. A short circuit is a path with no bulb at all.

flow.context: In this step, you draw the circuits that you built in Bulb Teams as diagrams.

flow.do: Swap diagrams with a partner. Build the circuit that your partner drew, using only the diagram. Check that it lights. Write down any mistake in the diagram.
flow.say: Swap drawings with me. Build my circuit, using only my diagram. Does it light? If it does not, find out whether the mistake is in the drawing or in the building.
flow.kid: Swap diagrams. Build your partner's circuit. Does it light?
flow.parent: Mistakes are useful. A drawing with a gap, or a cell drawn with no wire to it, will not light. Let them find the fault themselves.
flow.context: In this step, you build a circuit from someone else's diagram, as an engineer would.

activities.title: Pencil Dimmer: slide the clip, change the glow

materials.item: a soft pencil, such as 4B or 6B
2 AA cells in a holder, 1 torch bulb of 2.5 volts in a holder, and 2 wires with crocodile clips
a craft knife or a blade, for a grown-up to use
a ruler

activities.safety: A grown-up shaves the pencil with a blade, cutting away from their body, on a table, with the pencil held flat. Children do not use the blade. Keep the bare lead away from clothes: it marks them.
activities.record: Draw the circuit and write what the bulb did when the clip was near and when it was far.
activities.context: In this activity, you use a pencil lead as a wire and slide a clip along it to dim a bulb.

setup.art: A pencil with the wood shaved from one side to show a strip of dark lead, held by a grown-up's hand, with a blade lying safely to the side.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up shaves one side of a pencil to show the lead.

setup.art: A circuit with cells, a bulb and a pencil lead, with a crocodile clip near one end of the lead and the bulb glowing brightly.
setup.caption: 2. Clip near the end: the bulb is bright.

setup.art: The same circuit with the clip slid to the far end of the lead and the bulb dim.
setup.caption: 3. Clip far away: more lead in the loop, and the bulb is dim.

flow.do: A grown-up carefully shaves the wood off one side of a pencil, to show about 12 centimetres of lead. Test the lead with a bulb and cells. If the bulb does not light, use a softer pencil.
flow.say: A pencil's lead is graphite. It carries electricity, but holds it back more than copper does. A grown-up will shave one side of the pencil to show the lead.
flow.kid: A grown-up shaves the pencil to show its lead. We will use the lead as a wire.
flow.parent: Use a blade away from the body (a sharpener cannot expose the lead). Shave only one side, so the lead stays held by the other half; the lead is brittle, so go slowly. A soft pencil such as 4B carries more current than an HB. Start with a 2B or 4B. If the bulb never lights, use a softer one. If it stays equally bright wherever the clip is, the lead is too good a conductor: try an HB.
flow.context: In this step, a grown-up prepares a pencil lead that you can use as a wire.

flow.do: Join a clip from the cell holder to one end of the lead. Join the bulb to the other clip, and touch it to the lead near the first clip. Slide it slowly away. Stop at 2, 5, 8 and 11 centimetres. Score the bulb from 0 to 5 each time. Write the scores in a table.
flow.say: Join the circuit through the pencil lead. Start with the clip near the first end. Slide it slowly along the lead. What does the bulb do as the clip moves away?
flow.kid: Slide the clip along the lead. Watch the bulb. What changes?

ask.q: What happens to the bulb as the clip moves away?
good: The longer the lead, the dimmer.

flow.parent: Typically the bulb glows less as more lead is in the loop, but how much depends on the pencil: a pencil lead is not a perfect dimmer. Press the clips firmly on the graphite. In a dim room the change is easier to see. If the change is too small, try a harder pencil, such as HB, or use two pencils end to end. If the bulb stays off, the lead is too hard or the loop is broken. With 2 to 4 children, one slides the clip, one measures, one scores and one writes the table; a second child can score without seeing the first score.
flow.context: In this step, you make a dimmer from a pencil lead and watch the bulb.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they saw and why. Then ask where in a home a dimmer or regulator is used.
flow.say: Tell me what you saw and why you think it happened. Where in our house does something change the brightness or speed with a knob?
flow.kid: Say what you saw, and why. Where at home is there a knob like this?
flow.parent: A strong answer says that more lead in the loop holds back the flow more, so less current reaches the bulb. A fan regulator and a light dimmer do the same job, in cleverer ways.
flow.context: In this step, you explain why the lead made the bulb dim.

activities.title: Fuse Test: why a fuse is a thin wire

materials.item: fine steel wool, a few strands of about 5 centimetres each (grade 0000 from a hardware or paint shop; a kitchen scrubber is too thick). Substitute: a strip of kitchen foil cut to a narrow neck, 2 millimetres wide
a 9 volt battery
a metal tray or a steel plate, and a bowl of water

activities.safety: A grown-up does all of this activity. The strand gets very hot and can burn skin and light paper. Use a metal tray, keep paper and cloth away, and have a bowl of water ready. Never do this with a wall socket, plug or phone charger. Sparks and tiny hot bits can fly: the adult keeps their face back, children watch from arm's length, and everyone stays at least one step from the tray. Steel wool fibres splinter skin, so wash hands after. The battery and the used strand stay hot for a minute.
activities.record: Draw the strand before and after, and write one sentence about why a fuse is a thin wire.
activities.context: In this activity, a grown-up shows how a thin wire heats up and melts first, as a fuse does.

setup.art: A metal tray on a table with a 9 volt battery, three thin strands of steel wool, and a bowl of water, with nothing flammable near.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up sets up on a metal tray, with water near.

setup.art: An adult's hand holding a thin steel wool strand across the two terminals of a 9 volt battery, with the strand glowing orange.
setup.caption: 2. The thin strand glows and breaks.

setup.art: A home wiring box with a row of small switches, and a child pointing at it from a few steps away.
setup.caption: 3. Find the MCB box at home. Look, do not touch.

flow.do: A grown-up sets up on a metal tray, away from paper, with a bowl of water nearby. Pull out a few strands of fine steel wool, about 5 centimetres long. Hold up one strand and a copper wire. Ask which will get hotter if the same current flows.
flow.say: Here is one thin strand of steel wool and one thick copper wire. If we send the same current through both, which one will get hotter? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A grown-up does this. Which gets hotter, the thin strand or the thick wire? Why?
flow.parent: Do this only with a grown-up in charge. Keep the children at arm's length: one child or several can watch, predict, and count seconds aloud, one holding the timer and one writing results. Use a metal tray, a 9 volt battery, and a bowl of water close by. No paper, cloth or plastic near the tray.
flow.context: In this step, you guess which is hotter, a thin strand or a thick wire.

flow.do: A grown-up lays one thin strand across the two terminals of a 9 volt battery, holding the battery by its sides. The strand typically glows orange and breaks in a second or two. Count the seconds aloud. Then twist 5 or 6 strands into one bundle and try again. It lasts longer. Put the used strands on the tray. Disconnect and put the battery away.
flow.say: Watch. The grown-up touches the strand across the battery. What happens to the thin strand? Now think: a fuse is a thin wire like this one, put in a circuit on purpose.
flow.kid: A grown-up touches the strand to the battery. Watch the strand. What happens?
flow.parent: Single thin strand: it typically glows and breaks within a second or two, often with a few sparks. The twisted bundle should last longer, which shows that thicker means more flow gets through before it melts. If nothing happens, the strand may be too thick or loose: use finer steel wool, press it onto both terminals, or try a fresh battery. If steel wool is not available, a foil strip with a narrow neck works in the same way. Do not hold it for long, because the battery gets warm. Never do this with a plug, wall socket or mobile phone charger. Let the strands cool on the tray, then put them in the bin.

check.q: A fuse in a plug is a thin wire. Why is it thin on purpose?
options: So that the plug is lighter
So that it heats up and melts first if the current gets too big
So that it uses less metal
check.why: A thin wire holds back the flow more than a thick one, so it heats first. When a fault makes the current too big, the thin wire melts and breaks the circuit before the thick house wires get hot.

flow.context: In this step, a thin strand of steel wool glows and breaks, as a fuse does.

flow.do: Ask your child where the fuse or MCB box is in your home. Find it together, without touching it. Ask who must do anything with it.
flow.say: Where is the fuse or MCB box in our house? Let us find it. It protects the wires in the walls. Who is allowed to touch it?
flow.kid: Find the MCB box at home. Look, do not touch. It protects the wires.
flow.parent: A fuse or MCB protects the wires, but it does not protect a person who touches a live wire. Only an adult resets an MCB, and only after finding out why it tripped.
flow.context: In this step, you find the fuse or MCB box in your home.

activities.title: Be the Festival Lights: a human circuit

materials.item: 4 or 5 people, or soft toys
a bag of 20 dry beans

activities.record: Draw the ring and the two lanes as circuit diagrams, and mark where the break was.
activities.context: In this activity, you act out a series circuit and a parallel circuit, and see what a break does to each.

setup.art: Five children standing in a ring, passing a small bag from one to the next, one child labelled cell and four labelled bulb.
setup.caption: 1. A ring of people passes a bag round. This is a series circuit.

setup.art: The same ring with one child sitting down and the bag stopped in the hands of the child before them.
setup.caption: 2. One bulb sits down, and the bag stops for everyone.

setup.art: Two lanes of children running from a cell child to a finish line and back, one bulb child in each lane, with one lane sitting down and the other still passing the bag.
setup.caption: 3. Two lanes: one lane breaks, the other carries on.

flow.do: Gather 5 people, or use toys as bulbs. Choose one person as the cell. Everyone else is a bulb. Give the cell a bag of 20 small things, such as dry beans, to be the charges.
flow.say: We are going to be a circuit. One person is the cell. The others are bulbs. The beans are the charges. The cell starts them moving round.
flow.kid: We are a circuit. One of us is the cell. The rest are bulbs.
flow.parent: With only two or three people, use soft toys or cushions as bulbs and let the child move the beans themselves. The beans are only for passing: they are not to be eaten, and keep them away from children under three who might swallow them.
flow.context: In this step, you choose who is the cell and who are the bulbs, and gather the beans.

flow.do: Make a ring. Pass one bag of beans from the cell, through each bulb in turn, and back to the cell. Everyone holds their hands out when the bag arrives. Now one bulb sits down and refuses to pass the bag. Watch what happens to the ring.
flow.say: This ring is a series circuit. The bag goes round, bulb to bulb. Now one bulb sits down. What happens to the bag? What happens to the others?
flow.kid: Make a ring. Pass the bag round. One bulb sits down. What happens?

ask.q: What happened when one person sat down?

flow.parent: The bag stops at the one who sat down, and everyone behind has nothing to pass. This is why one broken bulb darkens a whole series string.
flow.context: In this step, you act out a series circuit and then break it.

flow.do: Now make two lanes from the cell to a finish line and back, one bulb in each lane. The cell hands out two bags at the same time, one for each lane. One bulb sits down. Watch the other lane. Count how many beans the cell hands out in 30 seconds, first in the ring and then with the two lanes.
flow.say: Now each bulb has its own lane. The cell hands a bag to each lane. One bulb sits down. What does the other lane do? What is the cell doing now compared with before?
flow.kid: Make two lanes. One bulb sits down. What does the other lane do?

ask.q: What is different for the cell now?
good: It has to hand out two bags at once.

flow.parent: The other lane carries on. The cell has to hand out two bags at once, so with two lanes it hands out about twice as many beans in the same 30 seconds as in the ring, which is why cells run down faster in parallel. Counts will not be exact. With one child and one parent, use toys for the bulbs and count the beans yourselves.

check.q: In your acting, one lane's bulb sat down and the other lane carried on. What does that show about a parallel circuit?
options: The cell stops working
A break anywhere stops everything
A break in one branch leaves the other branches working
check.why: Each lane has its own path from the cell and back. Breaking one lane leaves the other lane's loop whole. In a series ring, one person sitting down stops everyone.

flow.context: In this step, you act out a parallel circuit and break one branch.

projects.title: Build a Three-Bulb Festival String

materials.item: 2 AA cells in a holder
3 torch bulbs of 2.5 volts in holders
a piece of cardboard about 30 centimetres by 20 centimetres
kitchen foil strips, or about 8 wires, and sticky tape
a switch, or a paper clip and a drawing pin on a card, for a home-made switch
paper, a pencil and a ruler

projects.safety: Use only AA cells. Keep the two rails apart so they never touch. Small parts such as drawing pins stay away from children under five. Wires and cells may get warm if the rails touch: open the switch and take them apart at once. Open the switch when you are not testing, because the cells run down fast.
projects.record: Keep the circuit diagram. Write a table of the two strings: brightness, and what the others do when one is unscrewed.
projects.context: In this project, you build a small festival string where each bulb has its own path, and compare it with a string wired in a row.

setup.art: A circuit diagram on paper showing a cell, a switch in the main wire, and three bulbs on three branches side by side.
setup.caption: 1. Draw your string. The switch goes in the main wire.

setup.art: A piece of cardboard with two long foil strips taped along it as rails, and three bulb holders placed across the rails.
setup.caption: 2. Lay two rails and place the bulbs across them.

setup.art: A finished string on cardboard with three bulbs glowing and a hand unscrewing one bulb while the other two stay lit.
setup.caption: 3. Test it. Unscrew one bulb. The others stay lit.

flow.do: Draw a circuit diagram of the string you will build. It has a cell holder, a switch, and three bulbs side by side. Put the switch in the main wire. Check that each bulb has its own path.
flow.say: We will build a small festival string where each bulb has its own path. First draw it with symbols. Put the switch where it can turn all three off at once. Where must it go?
flow.kid: Draw your string with symbols. Three bulbs side by side. One switch for all.

ask.q: Where does the switch go so that it turns all three bulbs off at once?
good: In the main wire, before the bulbs split.
In the part that all three paths share.

flow.parent: The switch goes in a wire that carries all the current: next to the cell holder, before the paths split. A switch in one branch would turn off only one bulb.
flow.context: In this step, you draw the circuit before you build it.

flow.do: Stick two long foil strips along a piece of cardboard, or lay two long wires. These are the two rails. Join the cell holder to the rails at one end, with the switch in one wire. Place three bulb holders across the rails, each joined to both rails.
flow.say: Lay two long rails along the cardboard. Join the cells to one end, with the switch in one wire. Then join each bulb across both rails. Each bulb has its own path between the rails.
flow.kid: Lay two rails on the cardboard. Join the cells at one end. Put three bulbs across the rails.
flow.parent: If you use foil strips, fold the strip over the bulb holder terminals and tape it down firmly. Make sure the two rails never touch each other, or the cells will short out and get hot. Keep the rails about 5 centimetres apart. Test each bulb by itself before the switch goes in. Kitchen foil tears and loses contact easily: fold it into a wide double strip, or use wires with crocodile clips for the rails instead. Fresh alkaline AA cells give a brighter glow: three bulbs side by side draw about three times the current of one, so old cells make them dim. With 2 to 4 children, one lays the rails, one wires the bulbs, one fits the switch and one tests.
flow.context: In this step, you build the main part of the string on a piece of cardboard.

flow.do: Close the switch. Check that all three bulbs light. Open the switch. Unscrew one bulb, close the switch again, and check that the others stay lit. Write down what you saw.
flow.say: Close the switch. Do all three glow? Now unscrew one bulb. What do the other two do? Does this string behave like the old string in the story, or differently?
flow.kid: Close the switch. Do all three glow? Unscrew one bulb. What do the others do?
flow.parent: All three bulbs should glow about as bright as one bulb alone. The cells run down faster than for one bulb, so open the switch when you are not testing.

check.q: You unscrew one bulb from your string. The other two keep glowing. What does that show?
options: Each bulb has its own path from the cells
The unscrewed bulb was never used
The cells are very strong
check.why: In a parallel circuit, each branch is a whole loop on its own. Taking one out leaves the other loops whole. Strong cells would not make a difference to this. In a row, taking one out would put all of them out.

flow.context: In this step, you test your string, and take a bulb out to see that the others stay lit.

flow.do: Now build a second string with the three bulbs in a row, with the same cells and switch. Compare the two strings: brightness, and what happens when you unscrew one bulb. Make a table of your findings.
flow.say: Now build the same three bulbs in a row. How bright are they? What happens when you unscrew one? Which string would you hang across the lane, and why?
flow.kid: Build three bulbs in a row. Compare it with your first string. Which is better?
flow.parent: The side-by-side string is brighter and survives a broken bulb. But it needs more wire, and the cells run down faster. Real strings are often a mix: small groups of bulbs in a row, with the groups side by side.
flow.think: What is the price of a string where every bulb has its own path?
flow.context: In this step, you compare the string with a series string, and decide which is better for a festival.

challenges.title: Two Doors, One Bell: switches in a row and side by side
challenges.problem: Make two circuits using a cell holder, a bulb or buzzer and two switches. In the first, the bulb must light when either switch is pressed. In the second, the bulb must light only when both switches are pressed.
constraints: Use exactly two switches in each circuit.
Draw the circuit diagram before you build.
Test every combination: neither switch, one switch, the other switch, and both.
materials: a torch bulb (a 3 volt buzzer from a toy or electronics shop also works, but a bulb is easier to find)
2 switches, or paper clips with drawing pins on card
general: Two switches side by side for the 'either' circuit, like a doorbell with a front and a back button.
Two switches in a row for the 'both' circuit, like a safe that needs two keys.
A diagram first, then the build, then a table of every combination.
creative: A staircase light that can be switched on or off from the top or the bottom of the stairs, using two special switches.
A light that comes on when a door is open and it is dark, using a switch for the door and a light-sensitive part in a row (a light-sensitive part is hard to buy, so draw this one).
A three-door alarm: a bulb that lights if any one of three doors is opened.
challenges.your_turn: Invent a problem for your family: a rule about when a light should come on. Draw a circuit for it. Build it and test every combination. Which switches ended up in a row, and which side by side?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about switches. You make circuits that follow the rules 'both are needed' and 'either is enough'.

setup.art: A circuit diagram of a bulb, a cell, and two switches in one loop, one after the other.
setup.caption: 1. Switches in a row: both must be closed.

setup.art: A circuit diagram of a bulb, a cell, and two switches on two side-by-side branches.
setup.caption: 2. Switches side by side: either one is enough.

setup.art: A child pressing a home-made paper clip switch while a bulb glows, with a second paper clip switch beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Build and test every combination.

flow.do: Read the two problems together. Ask your child to sketch a circuit for each, using symbols, before they build anything.
flow.say: Here are two problems. A bell must ring when the front door button or the back door button is pressed. A safe light must come on only when two keys are both turned. Sketch a circuit for each.
flow.kid: Two problems. Sketch a circuit for each, with symbols.

ask.q: Which problem needs both switches, and which needs either?

flow.parent: Do not give the answer. Let them try. The bell has two switches side by side. The safe has two switches in a row.
flow.context: In this step, you read the problem and sketch your ideas.

flow.do: Build the bell circuit using a bulb or a buzzer, a cell holder and two switches side by side. Test it with each button on its own, then both.
flow.say: Build the door bell. Press the front button only. Press the back button only. Press both. When does it ring?
flow.kid: Build the door bell. Test each button, and then both.
flow.parent: Home-made switches work well: a paper clip held by a drawing pin on a card, pressed down onto a second pin. With 2 to 4 children, each pair builds one of the two circuits and then swaps to test the other. Two switches side by side means each is joined across the same two points.
flow.context: In this step, you build the two-door bell and test it.

flow.do: Build the safe light with two switches in a row. Test it with each switch on its own, then both. Write down when the light comes on.
flow.say: Now build the safe. Turn the first key only. Turn the second key only. Turn both. When does the light come on?
flow.kid: Build the safe light. Test each switch, and then both.
flow.parent: Two switches in a row means the electricity must pass through both, so both must be closed.

check.q: A circuit lights a bulb only when two switches are both closed. How are the switches joined?
options: One on each side of the cell with no wire between
In a row
Side by side
check.why: In a row, the only path goes through both switches, so both must be closed. Side by side, closing either one makes a path. A circuit with a switch on each side of a cell with no loop never lights.

flow.context: In this step, you build the two-key safe light and test it.

flow.do: Ask your child to design a third circuit of their own and test it. Then ask what computers do with millions of such switches.
flow.say: Now design your own. For example, a light that comes on when a door is open and it is dark. Which switches go in a row? Which go side by side?
flow.kid: Design your own switch circuit. Test it. Which switches are in a row?
flow.parent: Claude Shannon showed in 1937 that switch circuits like these can do logic. Computer chips join millions of tiny switches in rows and side by side.
flow.context: In this step, you design your own switch circuit.

quiz.p: Priya builds two circuits with the same cells and the same kind of bulbs. In circuit X, two bulbs are in a row. In circuit Y, they are side by side. Which bulbs glow brighter?
quiz.why: In circuit Y each bulb has its own path and gets the full push. In circuit X they share it, so each is dimmer.

quiz.p: In a home, a fan keeps spinning when you switch off the light beside it. Why?
opts: Each is on its own branch, so a switch controls only its own branch
quiz.why: Home wiring is parallel. A switch in one branch breaks only that branch. If the home were in a row, switching off one light would put out everything.

quiz.p: Three equal bulbs are in a row on cells that push with 6 volts. About how many volts does each bulb get?
quiz.why: The push is shared equally in a row. 6 volts divided between 3 bulbs is 2 volts each.

quiz.p: What makes a bulb's filament glow while the thick wires joined to it stay cool?
opts: The thick wires have no current in them
The filament is thin and holds back the flow a lot, so it gets very hot
quiz.why: The same current goes through both. Only the thin filament has high resistance, so the energy turns to heat and light there.

quiz.p: In a circuit diagram, which symbol stands for a cell?
opts: A long thin line next to a short fat line
A circle with a cross inside
quiz.why: The cell is a long thin line, the plus end, next to a short fat line, the minus end. The circle with a cross is a bulb, and the gap with a lever is a switch.

quiz.p: The arrow in a circuit diagram goes from the plus end of the cell round to the minus end. What is true about the electrons in a metal wire?
opts: They move the opposite way, from minus to plus
They move the same way as the arrow
They do not move at all
quiz.why: Franklin guessed the direction of the arrow in 1747. Later the electron was found, and it moves the other way.

quiz.p: An LED does not light when you join it to a coin cell. What should you try first?
opts: Join a second coin cell in a row
quiz.why: An LED works only one way round. Turned the right way, its long leg is on the plus face. The wrong way round it blocks the current but is not harmed. Two coin cells in a row could burn it out.

opts: It melts and breaks the circuit when the current gets too big
quiz.why: A fuse is a thin wire that heats first. It breaks the circuit before the wires in the walls get dangerously hot.

quiz.p: A loose wire touches both ends of a cell and quickly gets hot. What is this called?
quiz.why: Nothing holds back the flow except the wire, so the current is huge and the wire heats up. It is dangerous and the wire should be removed at once.

quiz.p: A safe light should come on only when two keys are both turned. How are the two key switches joined?
opts: On opposite sides of the bulb with no wire
quiz.why: In a row, the only path goes through both switches, so both must be closed.

quiz.p: A bell should ring if either of two buttons is pressed. How are the buttons joined?
opts: One button in the cell holder
quiz.why: Side by side, pressing either button makes a whole loop. Pressing both works too.

quiz.p: In two equal bulbs in a row, more current goes through the first bulb than the second.
quiz.why: False. The current is the same all round a series loop, so equal bulbs glow equally. They are dim because they share the push.

items.p: Two equal bulbs are joined in a row to one set of cells. Compared with one bulb alone, how bright is each bulb?
opts: As bright as one bulb alone
items.why: In a row, the two bulbs share the cells' push, and less current goes round the loop. Each bulb glows dimly.

items.p: Two equal bulbs are joined side by side to one set of cells. Compared with one bulb alone, how bright is each bulb?
opts: As bright as one bulb alone
items.why: Side by side, each bulb has its own path and gets the whole push of the cells. Each glows as brightly as a single bulb would.

items.p: In a row of equal bulbs, the first bulb is always the brightest.
items.why: False. The same current goes through every bulb in a row, so equal bulbs glow equally. The order along the wire makes no difference.

items.p: If you unscrew one bulb from a parallel circuit, the other bulbs stay lit.
items.why: True. Each bulb is on its own branch, so the other branches are still complete loops.

items.p: A circuit with only one path is called a ____ circuit.
items.why: Series means one after another, with one path. A break anywhere stops everything.

items.p: A circuit where each bulb has its own path to the cell is called a ____ circuit.
items.why: Parallel means side by side. Each bulb is on its own branch.

items.p: Match each circuit symbol to the part it stands for.
pairs: a circle with a cross inside
a long thin line next to a short fat line
items.why: Engineers all over the world use these same four symbols, so any diagram can be read anywhere. In the cell symbol, the long line is the plus end.

items.p: Sort each one by how its parts are wired.
items: an old festival string that goes dark when one bulb fails
a fan and a tube light in a room
a switch and the light it controls
the lights in different rooms of a home
three AA cells inside a torch
a front-door bell button and a back-door bell button that ring one bell
items.why: Where one break must stop everything, or where pushes add up, things are in a row. Where each part must work alone, they are side by side.

items.p: A fan keeps turning when you switch off the tube light in the same room. What does that show about how they are wired?
opts: They are on separate branches, side by side
The fan has its own cell
items.why: Switching off the tube light opens only its own branch. The fan's branch is still a complete loop, so the fan keeps turning.

items.p: Put these in order, from the dimmest bulbs to the brightest.
items.why: The more bulbs share the push in a row, the less each one gets. Three in a row are the dimmest, and one alone is the brightest.

items.p: What is the job of a fuse in a circuit?
opts: To melt and break the circuit if the current gets too big
items.why: A fuse is a thin wire that heats first. If a fault makes the current too big, it melts and breaks the circuit before the other wires get hot.

items.p: In your own words, explain why a bulb's thin filament glows but the thick copper wire joined to it stays cool.
items.a: The same current goes through both. The filament is very thin and holds back the flow a lot, so the charges give up much energy there as heat, and it gets hot enough to glow. The thick wire holds back the flow very little, so it stays cool.
items.why: A strong answer says the current is the same in both, that the filament has high resistance, and that this is where the energy turns to heat and light.

items.p: Draw a circuit diagram of one cell and two bulbs side by side. Use the symbols and mark the plus end of the cell.
items.a: A cell with two bulbs on two separate branches between the same two points, drawn with a ruler, with the long line of the cell marked plus.
items.why: A strong diagram shows two branches, one bulb on each, joined at both ends to the cell. If the bulbs are on one loop, the circuit is in series.

items.p: Here is a circuit diagram of a cell, a switch and a bulb in one loop. Label each part.
a: a long thin line next to a short fat line: cell
a gap with a lever: switch
a circle with a cross: bulb
items.why: Each part has its own symbol: the cell is a long thin line beside a short fat one, the switch is a gap with a lever, and the bulb is a circle with a cross.
items.art: A neat circuit diagram of a cell, an open switch and a bulb joined in one square loop, with a blank label box beside each part.

items.p: You join an LED to a coin cell and it does not light. When you turn it round, it lights. What was wrong the first time?
opts: It was joined the wrong way round
items.why: An LED lets current through one way only. Turned round, it simply blocks the current. It is not damaged, and the cell was fine since it lit afterwards.

items.p: Three equal bulbs are joined in a row to cells that push with 4.5 volts. About how many volts does each bulb get?
items.why: In a row, the push is shared. 4.5 volts shared between 3 equal bulbs is 1.5 volts each.

items.p: What is the best reason that two bulbs in a row are dimmer than one bulb alone?
opts: The first bulb uses up the electricity
They share the push of the cells, and less current goes round
items.why: The same current goes through both bulbs, so the first does not use it up. Each bulb gets only a share of the push, and the extra bulb makes the path harder, so the current is smaller.

items.p: In a row of bulbs, there is less current after the first bulb than before it.
items.why: False. The current is the same everywhere in a series loop. If it were smaller after the first bulb, charges would be piling up or disappearing.

items.p: A wire joined straight across the two ends of a cell makes a ____ circuit.
items.why: Nothing holds back the flow, so the current is huge and the wire and cell heat up fast.

items.p: A torch has 3 AA cells in a row, all facing the same way. Each cell pushes with 1.5 volts. How many volts is the push?
items.why: In a row, the pushes add up. 1.5 plus 1.5 plus 1.5 is 4.5 volts.

items.p: A cell lasts 20 hours with one bulb. About how many hours does it last with 4 equal bulbs side by side?
items.why: Side by side, each bulb draws its own current from the cell, so 4 bulbs drain it 4 times as fast. 20 divided by 4 is 5 hours.

items.p: Three of these are wired side by side. Which one is the odd one out?
opts: the lights in different rooms of a home
an old festival string that goes dark when one bulb fails
two doorbell buttons that ring the same bell
a fan and a tube light in one room
items.why: The old festival string has its bulbs in a row, with one path. The other three each have separate branches, so they work alone.

items.p: Why do engineers still draw the arrow of current from plus to minus, when the electrons really move from minus to plus?
opts: Millions of diagrams and rules already use it, and the answers are right either way
Nobody has found out which way the electrons move
The electrons switch direction every second
items.why: Franklin guessed the direction in 1747, long before electrons were found. Keeping the rule means old and new diagrams agree, and the results come out right.

items.p: Zoya says: 'The first bulb in a row uses up some of the electricity, so the second bulb is dimmer.' Explain what is wrong with her idea.
items.a: In a row the same current goes through every bulb, so nothing is used up on the way. If the second bulb were dimmer, equal bulbs would not glow equally, but they do. Both bulbs are dim because they share the cells' push.
items.why: A strong answer uses what was seen: both bulbs glowed equally, which shows the same current reached both.

items.p: A bulb is joined to cells through a pencil lead. A short length of lead in the loop gives a bright bulb, and a long length gives a dim one. Explain why.
items.a: Graphite holds back the flow of electricity. More lead in the loop holds it back more, so less current reaches the bulb, and the bulb is dimmer.
items.why: A strong answer uses the word resistance, and says that a longer lead has more of it.

items.p: Draw a circuit with a cell, a bulb and two switches so that the bulb lights only when both switches are closed. Use the symbols.
items.a: A cell, a bulb and two switches all in one loop, one after the other.
items.why: Both switches are on the only path, so both must be closed for the loop to be whole.

items.p: Here is a circuit diagram of two bulbs side by side with a cell. Label the cell, the two branches and the two bulbs.
a: the long and short lines: cell
the bulb on branch 1: bulb A
the bulb on branch 2: bulb B
items.why: Each bulb is on its own branch. The two branches start and end at the same two points, joined to the cell.
items.art: A circuit diagram of a cell with two branches between the same two points, a bulb on each branch, and a blank label box beside each part.

items.p: A family is deciding how to wire the new festival lights on their balcony.

views.says: Put the bulbs in a row. It needs less wire, and if one fails we can find it and swap it.
Put every bulb side by side. One broken bulb leaves the rest lit, and every bulb is bright.
Use small groups of bulbs in a row, and put the groups side by side.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with most? Give a reason from this unit. Then say one thing another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a view and backs it with a fact, such as: a row breaks all at once, side by side stays lit, a mix saves wire and limits the damage. It also gives one fair point for another view.
items.why: There is no single right answer. Each wiring has a price. Series needs less wire but fails together. Parallel is steady but uses more wire and drains the cells faster.

items.p: An electrician puts a much bigger fuse in a house circuit than the wires can safely carry. What is the danger?
opts: The fuse will melt too soon
The wires could overheat and start a fire before the fuse melts
items.why: A fuse protects the wires by melting before they get too hot. A fuse that is too big does not melt in time.

items.p: Why is a bulb's filament made so thin?
opts: A thin wire carries more current
A thin wire is cheaper to see
A thin wire holds back the flow, so it gets hot enough to glow
items.why: A thin wire has high resistance. The charges give up their energy there as heat, which makes it glow.

items.p: Two cells are joined in a row but facing opposite ways, with a bulb. What does the bulb do?
opts: It glows as bright as with one cell
It stays dark, because the pushes cancel
items.why: Cells in a row add their pushes only if they face the same way. Facing opposite ways, the pushes work against each other and cancel.

items.p: A string has 100 equal bulbs in a row, joined to the 230 volts of the mains. About how many volts does each bulb get?
items.why: The push is shared equally. 230 divided by 100 is 2.3 volts each.

items.p: One cell, with one bulb, lasts 10 hours. Now two cells are joined side by side and run two bulbs side by side. About how many hours does the pair of cells last?
items.why: Each bulb draws the same current as before. The two cells share the load, so each cell gives out only what it did when it ran one bulb. Each lasts about 10 hours.

items.p: A fuse protects a person who is touching a live wire.
items.why: False. A fuse protects the wires from overheating. It can take too long to melt to save a person, so electrical safety rules for people still apply.

items.p: In a circuit diagram, the arrow for current leaves the ____ end of the cell.
items.why: The arrow follows the rule Franklin guessed in 1747. The electrons really move the other way.

items.p: Match each wiring to what it does.
pairs: two switches in a row with a bulb
the bulb lights only when both are closed
two switches side by side with a bulb
the bulb lights when either one is closed
a switch in the main wire of a string with its bulbs side by side
a switch in one branch of a string with its bulbs side by side
turns off only that branch's bulb
items.why: Where a switch sits in the circuit decides what it controls. Whatever is in the same path as the switch is controlled by it.

items.p: Three of these are made to heat up or break when the current gets too big. Which one is the odd one out?
opts: a thick copper wire in a house
items.why: A fuse, an MCB and a filament are made to heat or break. A thick copper wire is made to hold back the current as little as possible so it stays cool.

items.p: Why does a wire joined straight across a cell get hot so fast?
opts: The cell makes heat on its own
Nothing holds back the flow, so a huge current goes through the thin wire
items.why: A short circuit has almost no resistance, so the current is very large. A large current heats even a thick wire.

items.p: An old festival string goes dark when one bulb fails. Explain, step by step, how you would find the broken bulb and fix it safely.
items.a: First a grown-up unplugs the string. Then look into each bulb with a torch for a gap in the thread, or swap each bulb with a spare one. Replace the broken bulb, check the plug and the wire, and plug in again.
items.why: A strong answer starts with unplugging, since mains is 230 volts. It then finds the one bulb that broke the path. Everything lights again when it is replaced.

items.p: A friend says: 'An electron races from the cell to the bulb really fast, which is why the bulb lights at once.' Is she right? Explain.
items.a: Not quite. The electrons in a wire drift very slowly, less than a millimetre in a second. The wire is already full of electrons. The push from the cell passes along the wire almost at once and sets all of them moving together, so the bulb lights straight away.
items.why: A strong answer separates the slow drift of the electrons from the fast push that passes along the wire, like a row of marbles in a tube.

items.p: Draw a circuit diagram of a home with a light, a fan and a socket, each on its own branch with its own switch, so that each can be used alone.
items.a: Two supply lines with three branches between them: one with a switch and a light, one with a switch and a fan, one with a switch and a socket.
items.why: Each part is on its own branch and its switch is in the same branch, in a row with it. Opening one switch leaves the others working.

items.p: Here is a drawing of a torch bulb cut open. Label the glass, the filament, the two support wires and the metal base.
a: the tiny coil at the middle: filament
the two thick wires holding the coil: support wires
the screw part at the bottom: metal base
items.why: Current goes in through the base, along a support wire, through the thin filament and out through the other support wire. The filament is where it glows.
items.art: A torch bulb cut open in a drawing, showing the glass dome, a tiny coiled filament held between two thick support wires, and the metal screw base, each with a blank label box.

items.p: Two inventors and an engineer disagree about who should be remembered for the electric light bulb.

views.says: We made a lamp that lasted, and we built the whole system: wires, meters and a power station, so streets could use it.
I showed a working lamp with a carbon filament in 1878 and 1879, before the system was built.
In 1882 I patented a better way to make carbon filaments, which made lamps cheaper and longer lasting.

items.ask: Who do you think should get the credit? Give a reason. Then say one thing another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives a reason, such as the first working lamp, the whole system, or the improvement that made it practical. It also notes that the bulb came from many people.
items.why: Credit for an invention is often shared. Inventions are built by many people, and the best-known name is not always the only one.

items.p: A circuit must light a bulb if either a door switch or a hand switch is closed. How should the two switches be wired?
opts: Both on one side of the cell with no bulb between
items.why: Side by side, closing either switch makes a whole path. In a row, both would have to be closed.

items.p: A cell that runs three bulbs side by side will run down about three times as fast as the same cell running one bulb.
items.why: True. Each bulb on its own branch takes its own current, so the cell must give out three times as much each second.

applications: Wiring the lights, fans and sockets of a home in parallel, so each works alone at the full 230 volts.
Putting a switch in series with the light it controls, so that opening the switch breaks the loop.
Festival string lights, where bulbs are wired in a row, in groups, or side by side.
Fuses and MCBs, which protect house wiring from short circuits and overloads.
Torches and remote controls, which put cells in a row to add their pushes: 3 cells make 4.5 volts.
LED indicator lights on chargers and televisions, which work only one way round.
Computer chips, which join millions of tiny switches in rows and side by side to do logic, an idea shown by Claude Shannon in 1937.
India's national power grid, which joins power stations and cities side by side and can share power when one place fails.
Dimmers and fan regulators, which change the resistance in a loop to change the brightness or speed.

Engineers such as Hertha Ayrton (1854 to 1923), who in 1899 became the first woman member of the Institution of Electrical Engineers, and Rajeshwari Chatterjee (1922 to 2010), who built up microwave engineering at the Indian Institute of Science in Bengaluru.

open_questions.q: How do the electrical signals between billions of nerve cells become a thought or a feeling?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can follow the signals from nerve to nerve. Nobody yet knows how this adds up to what it feels like to think.

open_questions.q: Can a material carry electricity with no resistance at everyday temperatures?
open_questions.why_open: Superconductors, found in 1911, carry current with zero resistance, but only when very cold or under huge pressure. A material that works at room temperature and normal pressure has not been confirmed.

open_questions.q: Why does every electron carry exactly the same amount of charge?
open_questions.why_open: Physicists have measured the charge very precisely. Nobody has explained why it has this value, or why all electrons have the same one.

open_questions.q: How can a whole country store electricity from the Sun for use at night, cheaply and cleanly?
open_questions.why_open: Batteries, pumped water and other stores exist, but none is yet cheap and large enough everywhere. Engineers are still testing many ideas.

open_questions.q: How small can a working switch be?
open_questions.why_open: Chip makers now build switches only a few nanometres across. How small they can go, before quantum effects make them unreliable, is still being tested.

maths.problem: A festival string has 46 equal bulbs in a row, joined to the 230 volts of the mains. How many volts does each bulb get? A second string has 23 equal bulbs in a row. How many volts does each bulb get, and why is it more?
maths.answer: 5 volts each in the first string. 10 volts each in the second. With fewer bulbs, each bulb has a bigger share of the same push.
maths.explain: 230 divided by 46 is 5. 230 divided by 23 is 10. The same 230 volts is shared between fewer bulbs, so each share is bigger.
maths.context: This is about bulbs in a row sharing the cell's push, as the bulbs in Bulb Teams did.
maths.why_maths: Dividing shows how a push is shared among bulbs in a row, and lets you predict how bright each will be without building it.

maths.problem: One bulb on two cells gets 3 volts. Two bulbs in a row get 1.5 volts each. Three get 1 volt each. Four get 0.75 volts each. What do six bulbs in a row get each? What do you notice?
maths.answer: 0.5 volts each. Each time you add a bulb, the 3 volts is divided into more equal shares, so each share gets smaller, and by less each time.
maths.explain: Six equal shares of 3 volts is 3 divided by 6, which is 0.5. The shares go 3, 1.5, 1, 0.75, and so on. The drop is big at first and then smaller.
maths.context: This is about the push each bulb gets when more bulbs are added in a row to the same cells.
maths.why_maths: Spotting the pattern lets you predict a result you have not built, such as six bulbs, and explains why a long string in a row has to use tiny bulbs.

maths.problem: One cell lasts 12 hours with one bulb. Each extra bulb side by side drains it by the same amount again. How long does it last with 2 bulbs, 3 bulbs, 4 bulbs and 6 bulbs side by side? What pattern do you see?
maths.answer: 6 hours, 4 hours, 3 hours and 2 hours. The more bulbs, the shorter the time, and 12 divided by the number of bulbs gives the answer.
maths.explain: Two bulbs use the cell twice as fast, so 12 divided by 2 is 6 hours. Three bulbs: 12 divided by 3 is 4. Four: 3. Six: 2.
maths.context: This is about the cells running down faster when bulbs are side by side.
maths.why_maths: Ratio shows the price of a parallel circuit: each extra branch costs the cell as much again.

maths.problem: A cell lasts 10 hours with one torch bulb. Anika uses the torch for 15 minutes each evening. How many evenings does the cell last? How many evenings would it last with two bulbs side by side?
maths.answer: 40 evenings with one bulb, and 20 evenings with two bulbs side by side.
maths.explain: 10 hours is 600 minutes. 600 divided by 15 is 40. With two bulbs side by side the cell lasts half as long, so 20 evenings.
maths.context: This is about how long a cell lasts when bulbs are side by side.
maths.why_maths: Changing hours into minutes and dividing shows how long a cell will really last in everyday use, which the number of hours alone does not tell you.

maths.problem: Look at the chart. Which layouts scored the same as one bulb alone? Another child predicts that four bulbs in a row would score 0 or 1. Do you agree? Give a reason from the chart.
maths.answer: Two side by side and three side by side scored 5, the same as one bulb. Yes, a score of 0 or 1 is sensible: the score fell from 5 to 2 to 1 as bulbs were added in a row, so four in a row would be 1 or 0.
maths.explain: The chart shows 5 for one bulb, 2 for two in a row and 1 for three in a row. The scores go down each time a bulb is added, so four should be even lower. Side by side stays at 5 each time.
maths.context: This chart shows made-up scores from a Bulb Teams test: one bulb, then two and three bulbs in a row and side by side.
maths.why_maths: A bar chart makes the pattern easy to see, and a pattern lets you make a sensible prediction beyond the numbers you have.

maths.problem: Suppose an electric eel's body has 6,000 tiny cells in a row, and together they make about 600 volts. If every cell makes the same push, how much does each make? How many AA cells of 1.5 volts in a row would make 600 volts?
maths.answer: 0.1 volts for each of the eel's cells. 400 AA cells in a row.
maths.explain: 600 divided by 6,000 is 0.1 volts. 600 divided by 1.5 is 400 AA cells. The eel's cells are tiny, but there are many of them.
maths.context: This is about cells in a row adding up their pushes, as the three AA cells in a torch do.
maths.why_maths: Dividing a total push by the number of cells in a row shows how thousands of tiny pushes add up to a large one.
