roots.context: We have built circuits in rows and side by side, and seen the same bulb glow bright, dim or not at all. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: The same bulb was bright alone, dim in a row, and dark with a gap. The bulb never changed. What it did was set by the loop it sat in. So a bulb has no brightness of its own.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'a bright bulb' and 'a dim bulb', as if brightness belonged to the bulb the way its size does. That label hides that the same bulb glows differently when its loop changes.
deep_truth.evidence: In Bulb Teams, one bulb scored 5 alone and about 2 with a second bulb in a row. Side by side, it scored 5 again. Unscrewing one bulb put out the others in a row but not the others side by side.

three.who_am_i: Each nerve cell in your body fires or stays quiet depending on the signals from the nerve cells joined to it. Like a bulb, a nerve cell is set by its loop.
three.what_is_life: A Venus flytrap shuts their trap only if a hair inside is touched twice within about 20 seconds. That is like two switches in a row, where both must be pressed.
three.what_is_this_world: A whole city, and India's national grid, are bulbs and machines side by side. Each gets a full push, and each can be switched off alone.

roots.thread: A cell is one push. The loop turns that one push into many different jobs: a glow in a filament, a hum in a fan, a ring in a bell. How the push is shared out depends on how the parts are joined. In a row, the parts share one push like one plate shared by a line of people. Side by side, every part draws from the same source at once. The world is joined in both ways. Some things depend on a single chain, and others on many paths at once.

teachings.teaching: Whatever comes to be in dependence on other things has no self of its own. Nagarjuna called this emptiness, and meant that things exist through their conditions.
teachings.link: A bulb's glow comes to be through the cell, the wires and the other bulbs in its loop. Change the loop, and the glow changes. Nagarjuna said this is true of everything.

teachings.source: Thich Nhat Hanh, The Heart of Understanding, 1988, on interbeing
teachings.teaching: Look deeply at a sheet of paper and you can see the cloud, the rain, the tree and the logger inside the paper. Nothing exists by itself alone.
teachings.link: The light of a bulb contains the cell, the wire and the other bulbs of its loop, the way the paper contains the cloud.

science.text: In a series circuit the same current goes through every part and the cell's push is shared. In a parallel circuit each branch gets the full push. So a part's behaviour is set by how it is joined to the rest.
A nerve cell fires when the signals from the nerve cells joined to it add up enough. How these signals become a thought or a feeling is not known.

other_view.view: A bulb does have a property of its own, its resistance. Everything else follows from that and from the cell, with one equation. Saying that brightness belongs to the whole loop only means you must know all the parts, and it is not a deeper truth.

playtest: Read as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, but not yet tried at home, so the brightness scores below are what the physics predicts. Bulb Teams: with 2.5 volt bulbs on two fresh AA cells, one bulb is bright, two in a row glow dull orange, three in a row glow faintly or not at all, and bulbs side by side are as bright as one. The steps say what to do if nothing glows, and to score by eye in a dim room. Cells run down fast in the side-by-side layouts, so the steps say to disconnect after each test. Pencil Dimmer: this is the least certain activity. Soft pencils (4B, 6B) carry more current than hard ones. If the bulb never lights, use a softer pencil, and if the glow barely changes, use a harder one. It may need two or three tries. how_we_found_out.story: In 1747, Benjamin Franklin in Philadelphia studied how rubbing made things pull on each other. He pictured one invisible fluid of electricity that flowed into some things and out of others. He called having too much 'plus' and too little 'minus'. He could not tell which way the fluid really moved, so he guessed that it moved from plus to minus. Everyone after him drew their arrows that way. In 1897, J. J. Thomson in Cambridge bent beams in glass tubes with magnets and charged plates. He showed the beams were tiny particles carrying the kind of charge Franklin had called minus. These are electrons. Later work showed that the moving charges in a metal wire are electrons too. So in a wire they move from minus to plus, opposite to the arrows. Engineers kept Franklin's arrow, because every diagram and rule already used it, and the sums come out right.
how_we_found_out.who: Benjamin Franklin in Philadelphia, and J. J. Thomson in Cambridge
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Franklin guessed that the electric fluid moves from plus to minus, and everyone drew their circuits that way. Thomson's electron showed that the moving charges in a wire go from minus to plus.
